<reason>B won by maintaining superior scope discipline, correctly distinguishing AI dubbing (faithful translation of existing performances) from voice cloning (generating new dialogue), which A repeatedly conflated. B successfully exposed that A's opt-in requirement collapses into either redundancy (if equivalent to a specific contract clause negotiated at hiring) or harm (if it creates a genuine perpetual veto). B also devastated A's protective stance by forcing A to admit that the remedy for withheld consent is replacing the actor—thereby harming the very supporting performers A claimed to protect. While A made strong consent-theory arguments about "consent by ambush," they failed to keep the debate focused on the proposition as written and could not answer B's redundancy challenge without conceding that better boilerplate might suffice.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (Turn 8) was decisive: by answering the pressure questions with a sharp distinction between "clarity" (specific contract language) and "separateness" (opt-in as a distinct refusable gate), B trapped A into admitting that opt-in negotiated once upfront is materially similar to an express clause, while simultaneously exposing A's replacement solution as a harm to lesser-known actors. This false-dilemma framing carried through to B's closing and sealed the argument.</best_rebuttal>
